title: Allocation fee lookups fail after a namespace move
telemetry: Supplied sanitized GKE console metadata, allocation-engine application logs (k8s_container) and dashboards, application-owner resolver-stage extracts and a same-Pod diagnostic, and platform-owner GKE network policy logging (policy-action log on k8s_node), NetworkPolicy summaries and Cloud DNS record checks. Static console-observation profile with no kubectl, cluster credentials, Pod exec, node access or cloud CLI. The example GKE version is a synthetic snapshot and makes no current-support claim.
owner: Wrenna, Allocations on-call, owns the investigation; Anselm, the allocation-engine application owner, owns its code, configuration and rollout; Perpetua, the fee-schedule service owner, owns the pricing-ref move in change CHG-8846; Calloway, the GKE platform and network-policy owner, owns cluster DNS, the pricing-ref NetworkPolicies, namespace labels and network policy logging. ITO coordinates the existing TLC and change approvals.
task: Wrenna has asked you to investigate why allocation-engine in cluster allocation-platform, namespace trade-allocation, project synthetic-allocations-prod, us-east4, stopped completing fee-schedule calls at about 13:06 UTC. Review the supplied observations for 2026-10-14 13:00-13:35 UTC and return a bounded technical finding with evidence, remaining unknowns and the next useful check with its owner, keeping namespace, Service and network-policy scope explicit. Keep the existing TLC as the coordination channel. No change is approved.

sources.claim: A normal Service gets an A/AAAA record my-svc.my-namespace.svc.cluster-domain that resolves to its cluster IP. DNS queries that do not specify a namespace are limited to the querying Pod's namespace, and the kubelet-written search list expands a short name to name.<pod namespace>.svc.cluster.local, so a Pod in another namespace must name the Service's namespace. The resolver extract reports only each lookup's final answer, so the case does not depend on GKE's exact search list or ndots handling.

A Pod is isolated for ingress when any NetworkPolicy with Ingress in policyTypes selects it; policies are additive allow lists with no explicit deny, and a connection needs both the source's egress and the destination's ingress to allow it. A default-deny-ingress policy does not affect egress, while a default-deny egress policy also blocks DNS unless DNS egress is allowed. namespaceSelector matches namespace labels. Variant B's policies are ingress-only in pricing-ref and no policy selects the client Pods, so client DNS is unrestricted by policy in both arms and resolution cannot fail because of them.

Network policy logging requires GKE Dataplane V2 and is configured by the single NetworkLogging object (default) with separate allow and deny log/delegate settings. Entries use log name policy-action on resource k8s_node, with connection fields (src_ip, dest_ip, ports, protocol, direction), disposition allow or deny, src/dest pod_name, namespace, workload_name and workload_kind, and count. The policies field appears only for allowed connections; denied connections are aggregated over five seconds and name no policy. The page does not say whether dest_ip records a Service ClusterIP or a Pod IP, so the supplied summaries give destination Pod and port and the case does not rely on dest_ip.
Kubernetes NetworkPolicy is always on in clusters with GKE Dataplane V2, network policy logging is built in, and Dataplane V2 can only be enabled when the cluster is created.

Cloud DNS for GKE manages DNS records for Kubernetes Services and can replace kube-dns as the provider; cluster scope, the default, limits Service-name resolution to the cluster, and kube-dns continues to run after Cloud DNS is enabled. Standard-cluster Pods use nameserver 169.254.169.254, where the Cloud DNS data plane listens on port 53. The page does not document query logging for Pod lookups, so lookup outcomes come from an application-owner resolver extract and the case claims no Cloud DNS query-log fields.

Troubleshooting Cloud DNS in GKE includes verifying that the cluster's private zone contains the Service's A record and checking the Pod's resolver configuration; Pods that cannot reach Services may report 'no such host' or 'dial tcp: i/o timeout'. The fixture's application wrapper text is synthetic and is neither a Google message nor graded.

a.conclusion: allocation-engine still looks up the short name fee-schedule, which resolves only within trade-allocation. When the old Service there was deleted at 13:06:30Z, cluster DNS began answering NXDOMAIN and no connection was attempted. The pricing-ref Service name resolves, and the same Pod reaches its ClusterIP with an allow entry from allow-fee-schedule-clients and no denies from trade-allocation, so the new NetworkPolicies are not blocking this path. Why the effective setting kept the short name is unknown.

Perpetua and Calloway check whether any other workload still looks up fee-schedule from trade-allocation before any owner considers restoring the old Service as a mitigation; that is an owner decision, not an approved step.

After an approved correction, Wrenna confirms resolver answers for the pricing-ref name, allow entries for allocation-engine sources, successful fee lookups and the held-allocation backlog with Anselm.

From 13:06:31Z, when pricing-ref's new ingress policies took effect, connections from all three allocation-engine Pods to fee-schedule on TCP 8443 are logged as denied at ingress. allow-fee-schedule-clients admits namespaces labelled fee-schedule-client=true; settlement-ops has the label and is allowed, trade-allocation does not.
